title: Music in One Level
objective: After this level you can describe what turns sound into music: rhythm, melody and harmony.
summary: Every one of 315 societies studied makes music. Music is built from rhythm (when sounds happen), melody (a line of notes) and, in most Western music, harmony (notes at once).

cards.headline: Every society scientists have checked makes music. Every single one.
cards.body: In 2019, a Harvard-led team combed through records of 315 societies around the world. Music turned up in all of them, and lullabies and dance songs were everywhere. So what is this thing every human group makes? This level gives you the recipe.

cards.headline: Ingredient 1: rhythm, the when
cards.body: Britannica defines music as sounds combined for beauty of form or emotional expression, usually by a culture's standards of rhythm, melody and, in most Western music, harmony. Start with rhythm: the pattern of when sounds happen, long and short, over a steady beat. Clap along to a song you love without singing a note. What your hands are keeping is the song's rhythm.

items.label: Rhythm
points: Long and short, over a steady beat

items.label: Harmony
points: Two or more notes at the same time

cards.headline: Harmony is the optional extra
cards.body: Look again at that definition: rhythm and melody are there for music in general, but harmony only for most Western music. So harmony is a layer, not a requirement. Hum a tune alone in the shower and you're making music with two ingredients: a melody, the line of notes, riding on a rhythm. The next eight levels take the ingredients apart, starting with the raw material: sound itself.

mascot.line: Shower singers, take heart: two out of three ingredients is still music.

cards.headline: Music: mapped
learned: Music turned up in all 315 societies studied
Rhythm: when sounds happen, over a steady beat
Melody: single notes heard as one line
Harmony: notes at once, found in most Western music

questions.prompt: In the 2019 Harvard-led study of 315 societies, how many had music?

options.label: About half of them
options.rationale: Music turned up far more widely than that.

options.label: Mostly Western ones
options.rationale: The study spanned societies all over the world.

questions.explanation: Music appeared in every one of the 315 societies, and lullabies and dance songs were everywhere.

questions.prompt: You clap along to a song without singing a note. Which ingredient of music are you keeping?

options.label: Harmony
options.rationale: Harmony needs notes sounding at the same time.

options.label: Melody
options.rationale: Melody is the line of notes, and you dropped the notes.

options.label: Pitch
options.rationale: Claps don't carry a tune; they mark time.

questions.explanation: Rhythm is when sounds happen, long and short over a beat, which is exactly what clapping keeps.

questions.prompt: Someone hums a tune alone in the shower, with no chords. Which ingredients of music are they using?

options.label: Harmony only
options.rationale: One voice alone can't sound two notes at once.

options.label: None: without harmony it isn't music
options.rationale: Harmony is a layer found in most Western music, not a requirement.

options.label: Melody and harmony
options.rationale: Harmony needs two or more notes at once.

questions.explanation: A hummed tune is a melody riding on a rhythm. Harmony is the optional extra layer.
